evidence.label: Critical local smoothing for the three-dimensional wave equation

headline: A claimed proof of Sogge's local smoothing conjecture for waves in 3D space, including the critical case p = 3.
scope: The claim is for the Euclidean wave equation in three space dimensions, with every positive loss at p = 3. The lossless endpoint is not covered.
plain: A wave can briefly pile up its energy in small regions, so its size at one instant can be worse than its start. Averaging over a short stretch of time is conjectured to win back most of that loss. Sogge's conjecture says exactly how much is won back in each Lᵖ size measure. This paper claims the three-dimensional case, at the critical exponent p = 3 and then all p above 2. Consequences for Bochner–Riesz means and pointwise convergence follow.
doesNot: This does not prove the lossless estimate at p = 3, or local smoothing on curved manifolds.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Christopher Sogge, who introduced local smoothing
scorecard.significanceWhy: Local smoothing in three dimensions is a central open problem, and it implies Bochner–Riesz and other estimates in harmonic analysis.

explanation:
Take an initial wave f(x) = sin(Nx) with frequency N = 1000. Its derivative has size about N. A fractional derivative of order α scales it by about N^α. That is how Sobolev size measures smoothness. At one fixed time, a wave in three dimensions can lose 2(1/2 − 1/p) derivatives in Lᵖ size[2]. The Lᵖ norm is the p-th root of the integral of |f|ᵖ. At p = 3 the loss is 2 × 1/6 = 1/3. For N = 1000 that costs a factor of about 1000^(1/3) = 10.

Local smoothing asks what happens when you also average over a short time interval. Sogge's conjecture says the loss drops to just above max{0, 1 − 3/p}[3]. At p = 3 that is 0, so only an arbitrarily small loss should remain. A loss of 0.01 costs about 1000^0.01 ≈ 1.07, instead of 10. At p = 4, the loss should fall from 1/2 to 1/4. At p = 6 it should fall from 2/3 to 1/2. In each case the gain is 1/p, as the conjecture predicts for p ≥ 3[4].

Sogge introduced local smoothing in his work on circular maximal operators[15]. Wolff, Łaba and Garrigós–Seeger built wave-packet methods for large p. A wave packet is a piece of the wave that travels along a thin tube. Bourgain and Demeter's decoupling theorem gave the conjectured gain for p ≥ 4 in three dimensions[7]. In two dimensions, Guth, Wang and Zhang reached the critical exponent p = 4 with a sharp square-function estimate[10]. In three dimensions at p = 3, Gao, Liu, Miao and Xi reached every loss above 1/9[8]. Gan, He, Li and Wu's work gives losses above 1/12 there[9]. The remaining small fixed loss is the gap this paper addresses.

The paper claims the estimate at p = 3 with every positive loss ε[1]. Interpolation with easier bounds then gives the full range 2 < p < ∞. Together these claim to resolve Sogge's conjecture in three space dimensions[5]. The lossless case ε = 0 is not addressed[6]. The word Euclidean matters. On some curved manifolds, focusing geodesics force p ≥ 10/3 for the full gain[16].

The main obstacle is controlling how packets crowd together across many scales. The paper's central quantity is the entropy of a finite phase-space record[11]. Phase space tracks both the position and the direction of each packet. Entropy here measures how spread out those records are. The proof uses two outside inputs[12]. They are Ren and Wang's planar Furstenberg theorem and Guth, Wang and Zhang's wave-envelope theorem.

The paper also claims consequences. Maximal Bochner–Riesz means converge almost everywhere for 3 ≤ p < ∞ when δ > 1 − 3/p[14]. A maximal bound for the wave itself needs s > 1/3 at p = 3[13].

How sure is this? There is no Lean scope note for this result, so no computer proof checker has tested it. The paper is very long and relies on two recent outside theorems. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark if the proof holds, since it claims a central conjecture in three dimensions. It is one very long paper with no Lean scope note. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A gain in smoothness for a wave when its size is averaged over a short time interval.
The number of derivatives an estimate gives up, measured by powers of the frequency.
A measure of a function's size: the p-th root of the integral of its absolute value to the power p.
A piece of a wave concentrated along a thin tube in one direction.
An inequality that bounds a sum of wave pieces using their separate sizes.
The joint record of where a wave piece is and which direction it moves.
Ways to rebuild a function from its frequencies with a softened cut-off at the edge of a ball.
